Problem

Measure a mindset, before and after.

A Dutch training provider needed honest answers from students, and a way to prove to schools what changed.

My bet

An invitation, not an exam. A summary, not a spreadsheet.

A friendly five-minute scan for students, and a summary-first report for researchers.

What I shipped

Two products, one system.

Student web (down to 320px), admin dashboard, chart system, design system and dev-ready files, all in weekly sprints.

    Decision log

    Six calls that shaped the product

    Not a list of process steps. Each card is a real choice: what I picked, what I rejected, and why. Open one to see the screens behind it.

    01Present the scan as a test, or as an invitation?Invitation

    Rejected: a neutral survey form, the default for research tools, which reads like an exam to a 14-year-old.

    Chose: three moments as friendly cards with mascots, “about five minutes” and “there is no right or wrong” up front, plus a QR code so a whole class can start from the classroom screen.

    Why: the data is only as good as the honesty of the answers.

    02One long form, or a stepper?3-step stepper

    Rejected: one scrolling page with 23+ statements and the personal fields mixed in.

    Chose: a stepper of Personal details → Part 1 → Part 2. Personal details are dropdowns, not free text.

    Why: short steps feel finite, and structured answers (school, grade, programme) become the dashboard’s filters later. I designed both together as one data model.

    03A 1–5 scale with a neutral middle?1–6, no middle

    Rejected: a 5-point scale, where a tired student can park every answer on “3”.

    Chose: an even 1–6 scale, with “Totally disagree / Totally agree” repeated on every row.

    Why: it nudges a real lean without forcing extremes, and repeating the labels means nobody scrolls back up to remember what “4” meant.

    04One chart per statement, or summary first?Summary first

    Rejected: my own first version, with one big bar pair per statement and a collapsed icon sidebar. Accurate, but researchers scrolled through dozens of charts and lost track of where they were.

    Chose: a visible report tree and a summary page leading with absolute and relative change per dimension. Details are one click away.

    Why: start with the answer, then let people drill down.

    05Separate filter and compare screens?One builder

    Rejected: a filter panel plus a separate comparison tool.

    Chose: one filter panel with a “Compare with other” toggle that reveals a second, identical row. Each row has its own Clear all.

    Why: the team’s most common question was “how did this school do against the rest?”, so comparison had to be one click, not a new tool.

    06Who maintains the questions and the data?The team, not devs

    Rejected: questions hard-coded by developers, and data fixed with database scripts.

    Chose: admin screens to edit question sets and to browse, edit and delete responses, plus user roles with confirmation steps.

    Why: about 1,800 historical answers had to be imported and cleaned, and the question sets change between programmes.

    How I use AI now

    AI speeds up the research and the production. Judgement stays with me.

    On this project AI helped in two places: compressing desk research at the start, and rebuilding the Figma file into this NDA-safe, coded case study at the end. Everything between, from workshops and flows to the decisions themselves, was mine.

    ✦Desk researchChatGPT · Claude

    Summarised sources on designing for Dutch users, the European Accessibility Act and dashboard typography into a short brief.

    ✓Research → rulesMe

    I turned the brief into design rules (tone, speed, language, accessibility) and checked each source.

    ✎Design & sprintsMe · Figma

    Workshops, weekly sprints with the client, flows, the design system, both products and the handoff.

    ⌘Read the fileFigma MCP → Claude

    Claude reads the Figma file directly: pages, sections and research links, then exports the real frames.

    ◐NDA passClaude + me

    Logos, the client name, emails and schools blurred with a script. I checked every crop by eye.

    </>Build in codeClaude

    This page, the prototype hotspots, the animations and the PDF, written from my direction.

    What the AI did

    • Summarised research sources into a short brief
    • Read the 20-page Figma file and listed its frames
    • Exported 18 real screens and blurred the identifying details
    • Wrote the page, prototype logic, animations and PDF

    What I did

    • Ran the client workshops and the weekly sprint boards
    • Turned research into design rules and checked the sources
    • Designed both products and made every call in the decision log
    • Checked every blur, claim and credit. No invented metrics or quotes

    “AI makes the research faster. It doesn’t decide what the research means.”

    Evidence

    Designing for Dutch students

    Each cultural insight became a rule I could point to in a review, and one was set aside where it didn’t apply.

    InsightWhat it meansHow it shaped Lumen
    EfficiencyWasted time is frustrating“About five minutes” up front, a 3-step stepper, QR start in class
    TrustFewer trust signals and rules neededNo account for students, a light admin login, minimal confirmations
    Informal toneFormal wording feels distantWarm microcopy: “Great that you’re participating!”
    FunPlayful design lifts engagementMascots and bold colour, on student screens only
    LanguageMany prefer EnglishEnglish UI, with the team’s Dutch research terms kept
    PaymentsLocal methods like iDEALNot applicable: no payments in scope
    Iteration

    My first dashboard vs. the one we shipped

    Drag to compare. The first version had a collapsed icon sidebar and one chart per statement. The shipped version has a visible report tree and leads with the answer: change per dimension, before vs after.

    Version 1Shipped
    ⇆
    Design system

    Playful outside, disciplined inside

    One system serves both products. Teal and violet carry the brand. Four extra hues each belong to one learning dimension, so a colour always means the same thing in every chart.

    Students get five honest minutes. Schools get proof of what changed.

    What shipped

    • Student scan: pre, post and evaluation, desktop and 320px mobile
    • Admin report: summary, per-dimension, evaluation, norm group
    • Question, response and user management
    • Design system and a “Ready for Dev” file with every edge state

    What I learned

    Two audiences, two tones: mascots for students, a calm and dense workspace for analysts, with one system underneath.

    Sketch the summary view before the detail charts. My first dashboard showed everything. The shipped one starts with the answer.

    What I’d measure

    • Scan completion rate and median time
    • Share of “straight-line” answer patterns
    • Time for a researcher to produce a school report
    • How often Compare is used
